level1.text: The end of a long coil spring is shaken sideways, and a transverse wave with a frequency of $4.0\,\text{Hz}$ and a wavelength of $0.75\,\text{m}$ travels in the spring. What is the speed of the wave?
A loudspeaker plays a note whose frequency is $440\,\text{Hz}$. The sound travels in the air of the room at a speed of $343\,\text{m/s}$. How long is the wavelength of the sound?
In a taut rope a wave travels at a speed of $6.0\,\text{m/s}$, and the distance between the crests of the wave is $1.5\,\text{m}$. At what frequency is the end of the rope shaken?
The wave machine of an indoor wave pool makes waves whose period is $2.5\,\text{s}$ and wavelength $4.0\,\text{m}$. At what speed do the waves travel?
In a rope a wave travels at a speed of $4.8\,\text{m/s}$, and its wavelength is $1.2\,\text{m}$. What is the period of the wave?
A coil spring can be made to vibrate in two ways: its end can be pushed back and forth in the direction of the spring or shaken sideways. Which statement about a longitudinal wave is correct?
level1.answer: The points of the spring vibrate in the direction of propagation, and compressions and rarefactions form in the spring

choices.text: The points of the spring vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation, and crests and troughs form in the spring
choices.feedback: This describes a transverse wave, not a longitudinal one. In a longitudinal wave the points of the medium vibrate in the direction of propagation.

choices.text: The points of the spring travel along with the wave from the source to the receiver, and matter moves to the other end of the spring
choices.feedback: A wave does not carry matter with it. The points of the spring vibrate around their equilibrium positions and return to their places, and only the disturbance and energy move forward.

choices.text: The points of the spring vibrate in the direction of propagation, and compressions and rarefactions form in the spring
choices.feedback: Correct: in a longitudinal wave the points of the medium vibrate in the direction of propagation, so travelling compressions and rarefactions form in the spring. Sound in air is a similar wave.

choices.text: The points of the spring stay in place, and only the end of the spring vibrates
choices.feedback: As the wave passes, every point of the spring vibrates in turn around its equilibrium position. The disturbance travels through the whole spring, so not all points stay in place.

level1.text: The end of a taut rope is shaken steadily. Then the shaking frequency is doubled, but the rope and its tension stay the same. What happens to the wave?
level1.answer: The wavelength halves, because the speed stays the same and the wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency

choices.text: The wavelength halves, because the speed stays the same and the wavelength is the speed divided by the frequency
choices.feedback: Correct: the speed is determined by the rope, not by the movement of the hand. From the fundamental equation $\lambda = v/f$ it follows that when $f$ doubles and $v$ stays the same, $\lambda$ halves.

choices.text: The speed of the wave doubles, because more frequent shaking pushes the wave forward faster
choices.feedback: This is a common misconception. The speed is determined by the medium, that is, the rope and its tension, and the frequency does not change it. The frequency changes the wavelength.

choices.text: The wavelength stays the same, because the wavelength is determined by the material of the rope and not by the movement of the hand
choices.feedback: The wavelength is not determined by the rope alone. The speed is determined by the rope, but the wavelength is $\lambda = v/f$, so it also depends on the frequency of the source.

choices.text: The wavelength doubles, because more frequent shaking stretches the wave longer
choices.feedback: With more frequent shaking, twice as many crests start in the same time, but they travel the same distance. So the crests fit closer together and the wavelength becomes shorter.

level1.text: In a thunderstorm the lightning is seen practically at once, but the thunder is heard $4.0\,\text{s}$ later. The speed of sound in air is $343\,\text{m/s}$. How far away did the lightning strike? Give the answer in kilometres.

In a yard there is a long taut rope with a light red ribbon tied to its midpoint. The end of the rope is shaken steadily up and down, and a periodic wave travels along the rope. The values of the situation are example values.

The ribbon makes $12$ full oscillations in $8.0\,\text{s}$.

In a photograph of the rope the distance between successive crests is $1.2\,\text{m}$.

Reason which statements are true and which are false.

statements.text: The frequency of the wave is $1.5\,\text{Hz}$.
statements.feedback: True: the frequency is the number of oscillations per second, $f = 12 : 8.0\,\text{s}$, that is, $f = 1.5\,\text{Hz}$. The period is $T = \tfrac{1}{f} \approx 0.67\,\text{s}$.

statements.text: The wave travels along the rope at a speed of $1.8\,\text{m/s}$.
statements.feedback: True: according to the basic equation $v = f\lambda = 1.5\,\text{Hz} \cdot 1.2\,\text{m}$, that is, $v = 1.8\,\text{m/s}$. The distance between the crests in the photograph is the wavelength.

statements.text: The ribbon and the point of the rope under it move with the wave towards the other end of the rope.
statements.feedback: False: a wave carries energy but not matter. The ribbon and the point of the rope oscillate up and down around their equilibrium positions, but they do not travel forward.

statements.text: With the same tension, shaking twice as fast increases the speed to $3.6\,\text{m/s}$.
statements.feedback: False: the speed of a wave depends on the medium, that is, on the rope and its tension, not on the frequency. The speed stays $1.8\,\text{m/s}$, and the wavelength shortens to $0.60\,\text{m}$.

statements.text: In the $(t, y)$ graph of the ribbon the distance between successive peaks is $1.2\,\text{m}$.
statements.feedback: False: the horizontal axis of the $(t, y)$ graph is time, so the distance between the peaks is the period $T \approx 0.67\,\text{s}$. The wavelength $1.2\,\text{m}$ is read from the photograph, that is, from the $(x, y)$ graph.

level2.text: The graph shows the displacement of one point of a taut rope as a function of time when the end of the rope is shaken steadily. From a snapshot of the rope it has been measured that the distance between successive crests is $1.0\,\text{m}$. Read the necessary value from the graph. What is the speed of the wave?

A student shakes the end of a long skipping rope steadily and counts that the hand makes $18$ full swings in $12.0$ seconds. The distance between the crests of the rope is $1.40\,\text{m}$. What is the speed of the wave in the rope?

The sound of a loudspeaker at the edge of a pool travels in air at a speed of $343\,\text{m/s}$, and its wavelength in air is $0.750\,\text{m}$. The sound continues into water, where it travels at a speed of $1480\,\text{m/s}$. How long is the wavelength of the sound in water?

The longitudinal wave of an earthquake travels in the bedrock. A seismometer measures the frequency of the wave as $0.50\,\text{Hz}$, and the wavelength is $12\,\text{km}$. What is the speed of the wave in metres per second?

A longitudinal pulse travelling in a coil spring was filmed, and the position of the leading edge of the pulse was read from the frames. Example data is in the table. The position is measured from the zero mark of the measuring tape, and at the start of the filming the pulse was already slightly past the zero mark.

Draw the $(t, x)$ graph and fit a straight line to the points. What is the speed of the pulse?

Give the answer as the slope of the line.

level2.text:
A student studies a wave travelling in a taut rope. In the $(t, y)$ graph of one point of the rope the distance between successive peaks is $0.50\,\text{s}$. In a photograph of the rope, that is, in the $(x, y)$ graph, the distance between successive crests is $1.5\,\text{m}$.

The student solves: “The distance between the peaks is the wavelength, so $\lambda = 0.50\,\text{m}$. The distance between the crests is the period, so $T = 1.5\,\text{s}$. So $v = \lambda/T = 0.33\,\text{m/s}$.”

What is wrong in the student's solution? Calculate the correct speed of the wave.

The speed of sound is measured with two microphones that are on the same line as a loudspeaker. The loudspeaker makes a short click, and a meter shows the time that the click needs to travel the distance between the microphones.

Example data is in the table. The distance $d$ is the distance between the microphones and $\Delta t$ is the travel time of the sound between them.

Determine the speed of sound by calculating the slope of the line through the points $d = 0.50\,\text{m}$ and $d = 2.00\,\text{m}$. Justify why the slope is better than the quotient of a single row.

data.caption: Distance between the microphones and travel time (example data)

level3.text:
Two photographs are taken of a rope at an interval of $0.15\,\text{s}$.

In the first picture a crest is at $x = 0.60\,\text{m}$ and in the second at $x = 1.05\,\text{m}$, and between the pictures the crest has not had time to travel one wavelength. In both pictures the distance between successive crests is $1.20\,\text{m}$.

At what frequency is the end of the rope shaken? Also justify why the displacement of the crest is not a displacement of the matter of the rope.

One end of a long railway rail is struck with a hammer.

A listener at the other end of the rail hears two bangs: first the sound that came along the rail and $0.50\,\text{s}$ later the sound that came through the air. Sound travels in steel at a speed of $5100\,\text{m/s}$ and in air at $340\,\text{m/s}$.

How long is the rail? Justify why the same blow of the hammer produces two sounds that arrive at different times.

A wave goes round a stadium stand: every spectator stands up $0.050\,\text{s}$ later than the one sitting next to them and then sits down again.

The distance between adjacent seats is $0.55\,\text{m}$, and the length of the row going round the stand is $440\,\text{m}$.

How long does it take for the wave to go once round the stand? Justify why the wave travels although no spectator changes places.

Example data: a $12.0\,\text{m}$ long rope is tightened with different forces $F$, and a pulse made at the end of the rope travels the whole length of the rope in time $t$. The measurement results are in the table.

Calculate the speed of the pulse for each tension. Investigate whether the speed depends on the tension directly proportionally or in some other way.

The rope is shaken at a frequency of $5.0\,\text{Hz}$ when the tension is $30\,\text{N}$. What is the wavelength of the wave that forms? Justify why the wavelength would change if the rope were replaced with a thicker one but the frequency were kept the same.

Give the answer as the wavelength.

data.caption: Travel time of the pulse as a function of tension (example data)

level3.text:
Example data: a long rope consists of two parts of different thickness joined together. The end of the rope is shaken steadily at a frequency of $5.0\,\text{Hz}$, and the wavelength is measured in both parts. The results are in the table.

At the start of the shaking, a single pulse is made in the rope, and it travels first through the thin part and then through the thick part. The reflection of the pulse at the joint is ignored, and the pulse travels at a steady speed in both parts.

How long does the pulse take to travel the whole length of the rope? Justify why the frequency is the same in both parts but the wavelength is not.
